author: Gary Franchi
title: SUPREME COURT TAKES UP ASYLUM CASE: Cooking for Terrorists a 'Material Support'? | Next News Network
text:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday agreed to hear the Trump administration's challenge to a lower court ruling that overturned the deportation order of a Nigerian man who was forced to cook for the Unknown Gunmen, a militant group linked to political violence in Nigeria. The case, Blanche v. Ozurumba, will determine whether providing food to members of a terrorist organization constitutes "material support" under federal immigration law — a question that could reshape how broadly that bar is applied to asylum seekers.
At issue is Izuchukwu Ozurumba, who, according to court documents, traveled to a remote camp outside Lagos in 2022 for a job. He was hired as a cook but grew suspicious when the movements of young men at the camp matched reports of killings and arson in the area. His lawyers say he tried to leave but was prevented and made to work without pay. After six months, he escaped during a supply run and returned to Lagos. He later fled to Venezuela and crossed into the U.S. illegally in July 2023, where he applied for asylum.
An immigration judge denied his applications, ruling that the Unknown Gunmen qualify as a terrorist organization and that preparing meals for its members met the legal threshold for material support. The judge said feeding the group helped it meet "basic human needs" and that Ozurumba's claims of coercion did not exempt him from the restriction. He was deported to Nigeria in 2025, even as his appeal continued. The Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals, in a 2-1 ruling, overturned his deportation order and sent the case back to the Board of Immigration Appeals.
Judge James Wynn Jr., an Obama appointee, wrote the majority opinion, joined by Judge Nicole Berner, a Biden appointee. The judges concluded that although Ozurumba prepared thousands of meals for the group's leaders, his cooking did not provide resources that could be directly used or readily redirected toward terrorist operations. The Fourth Circuit did not decide whether the law contains an exception for assistance provided under duress, an issue the court previously addressed in a 2012 ruling that relied on Chevron deference.
The case comes two years after the Supreme Court overturned Chevron deference, a doctrine that required judges to defer to federal agencies' interpretations of ambiguous laws. The 2024 ruling gave judges greater authority to decide what those laws mean. The Trump administration, which has made cracking down on illegal immigration a central focus, is now asking the high court to reverse the Fourth Circuit's decision.
According to SCOTUSblog, the Supreme Court's docket is already dominated by immigration cases. Since late April, the court has granted review in seven immigration-related cases, and six remain on the oral argument docket. The outlet notes that the second Trump administration's heightened focus on immigration issues — and reinterpretation of certain detention and deportation policies — has fueled a surge in immigration lawsuits at all levels of the legal system.
The legal question is narrow but carries broad implications: What exactly counts as "material support" for terrorism? The Immigration and Nationality Act lists examples of prohibited assistance, including transportation, communications, housing, money, weapons and training, but it does not explicitly define what constitutes material support. The Supreme Court's decision in this case could clarify that definition, affecting not just asylum seekers but also other immigration proceedings.
The case is scheduled for oral argument in the 2026-27 term. The court's ruling will determine whether Ozurumba's deportation order stands and how broadly the material support bar can be applied to immigrants accused of supporting terrorism, even through seemingly ordinary services.
Our Take
This case is a perfect illustration of why the American people are fed up with a broken immigration system that prioritizes the rights of illegal aliens over the safety of American citizens. The facts here are simple: a man cooked for a terrorist organization. The Unknown Gunmen are known for horrific violence — killings, arson, and terror. Under the Trump administration's tough-on-immigration policies, that should have been the end of the story. Instead, two judges appointed by Barack Obama and Joe Biden decided that cooking thousands of meals for terrorists somehow doesn't count as material support.
Let that sink in. You can feed terrorists, help them meet their "basic human needs," and still be eligible for asylum in the United States, according to the Fourth Circuit. This is the kind of judicial activism that puts American lives at risk. The law is clear: if you provide material support to a terrorist organization, you are barred from asylum. It doesn't matter if you were the cook or the bomb-maker — you are still aiding and abetting the enemy.
The Trump administration is right to take this case to the Supreme Court. The justices now have a chance to correct this dangerous precedent and reaffirm that America will not be a safe haven for those who serve terrorist groups, no matter how small their role. The decision could set a precedent for countless other cases, sending a clear message that the United States will not tolerate any form of support for terrorism.
Patriots, this is why elections matter. The Trump administration is fighting tooth and nail to secure our borders and keep Americans safe. The radical Left and their activist judges will do everything they can to stop him. But we have the Constitution, the law, and the truth on our side. The Supreme Court must rule in favor of the administration and uphold the material support bar in its full force. Anything less is a betrayal of the American people.
